section: Why Not Just Use PubMed Alerts?
text:
Why Not Just Use PubMed Alerts?
PubMed alerts are a reasonable starting point, but they have a key limitation: they give you a flat, unsorted list. If you set up an alert for “inflammatory bowel disease,” every matching paper arrives in the same inbox pile - therapeutics next to epidemiology next to basic science - and you still have to read through everything to find what’s relevant to your work.
IBD LitMonitor takes a different approach. Instead of delivering a raw feed, it organizes papers into sub-fields so you can go straight to the topic area you care about and skip the rest. Each category is collapsible, so browsing the day’s literature takes minutes rather than a lengthy inbox triage.

NoteHow to Read This Report



Coverage: PubMed queries across a broad set of IBD topic groups, deduplicated - each paper appears exactly once in the most specific matching category.
Categorisation: Automatic and imperfect - a paper found by multiple queries is assigned to the most specific one (e.g. a vedolizumab trial in children goes to Pediatric IBD). For keyword search across all categories or papers from the past 30 days, use the Interactive Dashboard.
Study design badges RCT Meta-analysis Review are shown only when PubMed has explicitly assigned a publication type. Papers published within the last 1-2 weeks often don’t have a badge yet.
★ Flagship journals: Papers from Gut, Gastroenterology, Lancet, NEJM, JCC, and other leading GI journals are marked ★.

Microbiome & Immunology  (34 papers)



Mechanisms and therapeutic perspectives of mucosal glycosylation-innate immunity crosstalk in inflammatory bowel disease (Review).Review  International journal of molecular medicine  |  2026-10-30



Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a group of chronic, relapsing inflammatory disorders of the gastrointestinal tract, driven by a complex interplay of genetic susceptibility, environmental exposures, intestinal microbiota dysbiosis and immune dysregulation. In recent years, mucosal glycosylation has emerged as a fundamental molecular determinant of intestinal barrier integrity and function and is increasingly recognized as a key regulatory interface linking the microbiota with host immune responses. Concurrently, the innate immune system serves an important role in mucosal defense and inflammatory responses through pattern recognition receptor‑mediated signaling, and its aberrant activation represents a key driver of persistent inflammation in IBD. The present review systematically summarizes the bidirectional regulatory crosstalk between mucosal glycosylation and innate immunity. The mechanistic roles of glycosylation modifications are highlighted in pathogen recognition, inflammatory signal transduction, inflammasome activation and maintenance of mucosal barrier integrity. Conversely, it is discussed how innate immune activation regulates glycan biosynthesis and remodeling through inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress and major signaling pathways, thereby reshaping the mucosal glycome in disease contexts. On this basis, the dynamic alterations of glycosylation‑innate immunity interactions across different stages of IBD, including disease initiation, progression and relapse, are delineated, emphasizing their important role in sustaining chronic inflammation and driving tissue remodeling. In addition, emerging therapeutic strategies targeting glycosylation pathways, glycan‑lectin interactions, mucosal barrier restoration and microbiota modulation are summarized. The potential of glycomics, multi‑omics integration and glyco‑immune biomarkers in disease stratification and precision medicine are also discussed. By integrating perspectives from glycobiology and immunology, the present review aims to provide a conceptual framework and novel directions for mechanistic research and targeted therapy in IBD.


Liu X, Zhang T, Jin J, Song Y, Li M, Zhong H, Cai M, Ding S, Han X


DOI: 10.3892/ijmm.2026.6032  |  View on PubMed →





Pathobiont-directed mucosal immunotherapy targets Ruminococcus gnavus and remodels host-microbiota interactions in colitis.★  Gut microbes  |  2026-10-30



Disease-associated pathobionts are recurrently enriched in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), yet their causal contribution and selective therapeutic control remain incompletely defined. Here, through clinical microbiome profiling and causal animal studies, we identified Ruminococcus gnavus (Rg) as a key ulcerative colitis (UC)-associated pathobiont whose abundance positively correlates with intestinal oxidative stress and inflammatory levels. To selectively constrain Rg, we engineered CP-EV@Ca, an oral microbiota-directed mucosal immunotherapy that combines pathogen-specific immune targeting with redox modulation. CP-EV@Ca enhanced mucosal antigen presentation, promoted T follicular helper cell-germinal-center B-cell responses and induced robust Rg-specific secretory IgA (sIgA). CP-EV@Ca-induced mucosal immune responses, including enhanced Rg-specific sIgA production, were associated with increased immune coating and reduced Rg expansion. In both acute and chronic colitis models, CP-EV@Ca outperformed 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA), suppressing inflammation and restoring microbial, epithelial and immune homeostasis. These findings demonstrate that pathobiont-specific mucosal immunity can be harnessed to selectively constrain disease-associated bacteria and restore intestinal homeostasis.


Wang Z, Huang L, Liu X, Cheng X, Liang Y, Chen J, Ma R, Song W, Li X


DOI: 10.1080/19490976.2026.2754605  |  View on PubMed →





Plant-derived exosome-like nanoparticles as candidate nano-prebiotics: from structure-enabled delivery to host-microbiota interface remodeling.Review  Critical reviews in food science and nutrition  |  2026-10-29



Gut ecosystem homeostasis depends on coordinated interactions among commensal microorganisms, the mucosal barrier, and the immune system. Conventional prebiotics rely on selective utilization by host microorganisms, but their efficacy is shaped by baseline microbiota and disease-associated ecological constraints. Plant-derived exosome-like nanoparticles (PELNs) are naturally occurring membrane-bound nanoparticles characterized by source-dependent lipid interfaces and associated molecular components, including small RNAs, proteins, polysaccharides, and plant-derived metabolites. We evaluate selected PELNs within a provisional “candidate nano-prebiotic” framework that allows particle- or component-mediated mechanisms to coexist with microbial utilization of fermentable components without implying equivalence to consensus-defined prebiotics. We critically assess evidence for microbe-directed and host-mediated effects on microbial functions, microbiota-derived metabolites, epithelial barrier integrity, and mucosal immunity, particularly in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Current evidence remains heterogeneous and predominantly preclinical, with major uncertainties regarding particle identity, component-specific causality, in vivo fate, microbiota dependence, dose plausibility, and mechanistic generalizability. We further define conceptual boundaries among PELNs, conventional prebiotics, and engineered nano-prebiotics and identify priorities for standardization, causal testing, food-relevant exposure assessment, safety evaluation, and mechanistically informed human studies.


Huangfu W, Liu C, Liu M, Sun H, Zhu X, Li D, Cui Y, Wang Z, Liu B, Shi Y


DOI: 10.1080/10408398.2026.2753614  |  View on PubMed →





The potential role of dietary polyphenols in the management of gastrointestinal issues in autism spectrum disorder.Review  Critical reviews in food science and nutrition  |  2026-10-29



Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental condition, frequently comorbid with heterogeneous gastrointestinal (GI) pathologies, including Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS), Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), and functional motility disorders. Emerging evidence implicates the microbiota-gut-brain axis in the pathogenesis of these GI anomalies. Dietary polyphenols, characterized by potent antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuromodulatory properties, represent a promising candidate approach for exploring the management of these comorbid conditions. This review critically examines the proposed molecular mechanisms by which specific phenolic compounds (e.g., resveratrol, quercetin and curcumin) may mitigate GI symptoms in ASD. Mechanistically, preclinical evidence suggests that polyphenols may help restore intestinal barrier integrity by upregulating tight junction proteins, suppress mucosal inflammation via the downregulation of Nuclear Factor Kappa B (NF-κB)/NOD-like Receptor Family Pyrin Domain Containing 3(NLRP3) pathways, and regulate gut motility through enteric neurotransmitter modulation. However, direct clinical efficacy in individuals with ASD remains largely unproven. Future clinical directions are proposed, focusing on the incorporation of low-fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols (FODMAPs) natural food matrices and the development of controlled food fortification strategies over isolated high-dose supplementation. This work provides a theoretical foundation and a concise roadmap for advancing polyphenol-based dietary interventions in the management of GI pathophysiology in ASD.


Nogay NH


DOI: 10.1080/10408398.2026.2755720  |  View on PubMed →





The Crossroads Between the Kidney and Gastrointestinal Disorders: Core Curriculum 2026.Review  American journal of kidney diseases : the official journal of the National Kidney Foundation  |  2026-10-29



The kidney and gastrointestinal (GI) tract are closely linked through a bidirectional system involving complex interactions called the gut-kidney axis. Within this system, alterations in the gut microbiome can promote progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD) while uremic toxins from advanced kidney dysfunction can adversely affect intestinal health. Incretin hormones, particularly glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), play an important role in this gut-kidney signaling and will be explored here. We also examine how this physiology helps explain the connection between GI illness and IgA nephropathy, along with the kidney manifestations seen in inflammatory bowel disease. Furthermore, we will review how CKD and end-stage kidney disease increase the risk of GI disease and complicate its management, and how CKD therapies affect GI symptoms. In this AJKD Core Curriculum, we use a case-based format to illustrate the intricate interplay between the kidneys and the GI tract.


Stevens T, Salani M


DOI: 10.1053/j.ajkd.2026.08.005  |  View on PubMed →





Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis ProSci-246 Protects Mice from DSS-induced Inflammatory Bowel Disease by Modulating the Intestinal Metabolite Profile in Mice.  Probiotics and antimicrobial proteins  |  2026-10-28



Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) refers to a chronic and recurrent gastrointestinal disorder, placing a lifelong medical burden on millions of individuals globally. As commensal microorganisms residing in the human intestinal tract, probiotics are capable of safeguarding the intestinal barrier, suppressing inflammatory reactions, and sustaining the balance of intestinal microbiota, with no accompanying adverse effects. Accordingly, probiotics have gained attention as a safe therapeutic approach and a major research focus for IBD treatment. In this study, the effects of Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis ProSci-246 (ProSci-246) were investigated in mice with dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis. Three groups of mice (n = 8 per group) were used: normal control (NC group), DSS-induced colitis mice without bacterial administration (DSS group), and DSS-induced colitis mice gavaged with live ProSci-246 bacterial suspension (ProSci-246 group). ProSci-246 significantly alleviated DSS-induced colitis, as shown by significantly higher 30-day body weight, colon length-to-weight ratio, and serum anti-inflammatory factor levels, along with significantly lower Disease Activity Index (DAI) scores and serum pro-inflammatory factor levels in the ProSci-246 group compared with the DSS group. Furthermore, fecal metabolomic analysis showed that ProSci-246 intervention altered DSS-induced fecal metabolic profiles, affecting purine metabolism, the pentose phosphate pathway, and the vitamin B6 metabolism pathway in IBD mice. These findings provide a scientific basis and novel perspective for the potential application of ProSci-246 as an alternative probiotic for IBD prevention and treatment.


Zhai W, Jiao Y, Chen H, Li J, Chen Y


DOI: 10.1007/s12602-026-11032-8  |  View on PubMed →





Differential efficacy of interleukin-23 pathway inhibitors in ulcerative colitis according to disease extent: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials.  European journal of gastroenterology & hepatology  |  2026-10-27



Interleukin-23 (IL-23) pathway inhibitors have demonstrated efficacy for moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis. However, whether treatment response differs according to baseline disease extent remains unclear. We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CENTRAL from January 2015 through August 2026 for randomized placebo-controlled trials evaluating IL-23 pathway inhibitors in ulcerative colitis. Clinical remission during induction and maintenance therapy was pooled using Mantel-Haenszel fixed-effect models for limited versus extensive disease. Treatment-by-disease-extent interaction was evaluated using within-trial ratios of risk ratios (RRRs). Five randomized placebo-controlled trial programs were included, four contributed extent-stratified induction data, and three contributed maintenance data. During induction, IL-23 inhibitors increased clinical remission in limited disease [risk ratio: 2.58, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.94-3.43] and extensive disease (risk ratio: 2.25, 95% CI: 1.62-3.13), with no significant interaction (RRR: 0.80, 95% CI: 0.51-1.24, P = 0.31). During maintenance, treatment was effective in limited disease (risk ratio: 1.56, 95% CI: 1.28-1.89) and extensive disease (risk ratio: 3.42, 95% CI: 2.45-4.77), with significant interaction (RRR: 2.16, 95% CI: 1.47-3.19, P < 0.001). Sensitivity analyses restricted to selective IL-23p19 inhibitors yielded consistent results. IL-23 pathway inhibition is effective across disease extents in ulcerative colitis. Disease extent did not modify treatment efficacy during induction, whereas a greater relative treatment effect was observed in extensive disease during maintenance.


Kaur A, Verma A, Chan T, Evans J, Goren I


DOI: 10.1097/MEG.0000000000003316  |  View on PubMed →





Plant Polyphenol-Polysaccharide Complexes for Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Molecular Interactions, Nano-Delivery Design, and Translational Evidence.  Nutrition reviews  |  2026-10-27



Plant polyphenol-polysaccharide complexes (PPCs) combine polyphenol bioactivity with the protective, mucoadhesive, and microbiota-accessible properties of polysaccharides. However, the literature often groups chemically distinct polyphenols together, extrapolates structure-function relationships across nonequivalent carriers, and interprets concurrent microbiota or short-chain fatty acid changes as causal mechanisms. This review critically evaluated how molecular interactions and measurable structural attributes of PPCs influence gastrointestinal stability, colon-oriented release, biological effects relevant to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and translational readiness. Targeted searches of PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were completed through July 20, 2026. Peer-reviewed original studies and relevant reviews published in English were considered. Evidence was classified as direct PPC evidence, PPC-relevant formulation evidence, or non-PPC mechanistic and engineering evidence. Information on carrier chemistry, payload, structural attributes, release behavior, biological outcomes, and translational considerations was extracted. Quantitative findings were compared only when carrier chemistry, payload, test conditions, and outcomes were sufficiently aligned; heterogeneous data were not pooled. Non-covalent assembly and covalent conjugation can alter molecular organization, physicochemical stability, and release, but no universal relationship between degree of substitution and release is supported. Epigallocatechin-3-gallate, quercetin, and anthocyanins require compound-specific carrier selection. PPC and PPC-relevant interventions are associated with changes in NF-κB-related signaling, epithelial-barrier markers, microbiota composition, and individual short-chain fatty acids, whereas receptor- or microbiota-mediated causality remains largely unverified. Responsive platforms also differ in stability, release control, scale-up burden, and clinical readiness. PPC-based nano-delivery is a promising preclinical approach, but translation requires matched studies linking structure, properties, and release, mediator-level mechanistic validation, standardized characterization, reproducible manufacturing, formulation-specific safety assessment, and comparison with established IBD therapies.


Mu J, Ma F, Zheng X, Fan Y, Fu J


DOI: 10.1093/nutrit/nuag153  |  View on PubMed →





Bibliometric Analysis of Traditional Chinese Medicine-Derived Bioactive Constituents in Macrophage Polarization Regulation.  Journal of visualized experiments : JoVE  |  2026-10-27



Macrophage polarization contributes to inflammatory regulation, tumor immunity, tissue repair, and fibrosis. However, the knowledge structure, research evolution, and emerging pharmacological directions concerning the regulation of macrophage polarization by traditional Chinese medicine (TCM)-derived bioactive constituents have not been systematically characterized at the field level. English-language articles and reviews published between 1 January 2000 and 31 March 2026 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection. After screening, 478 records were analyzed using VOSviewer 1.6.20 and CiteSpace 6.3.R1 to characterize publication trends, contributors, collaboration networks, co-citation relationships, keyword clusters, and citation bursts. Publication output increased markedly after 2019 and accelerated from 2022. China contributed the largest number of publications, with TCM-focused universities and institutes forming the principal institutional network. Major research themes included M1/M2 polarization, inflammatory signaling, tumor-associated macrophages, inflammatory bowel disease, gut microbiota, fibrosis, wound healing, and network pharmacology. Flavonoids, polyphenols, saponins, polysaccharides, and alkaloids were the main constituent classes identified. Recent research increasingly links macrophage regulation with immunometabolism, disease-specific microenvironments, microbiota-metabolite interactions, and direct target validation. The findings map the development and pharmacological directions of this research field and highlight the need for chemical profiling, multi-omics, single-cell technologies, and experimental target validation to clarify the material basis, molecular mechanisms, and disease-context-dependent effects of representative constituents.


Guo W, Zheng H, Han N, Liu L, Cheng Z, Jin P, Li Y, Jia Z


DOI: 10.3791/74315  |  View on PubMed →





Baseline microbial ecology encodes probiotic responsiveness through distinct metabolic and network configurations.★  Cell reports  |  2026-10-26



Probiotic efficacy in inflammatory bowel disease varies widely between individuals, and the sources of that variability remain poorly understood. D-lactate is a microbiota-derived metabolite that accumulates during intestinal inflammation and is associated with epithelial barrier dysfunction, which motivated our use of a consortium selected to contribute none of it. Here we show that its benefit is not an intrinsic property of the administered strains but is determined by the pre-existing ecological state of the recipient microbiome. Across three independent mouse resources, preventive administration reduced disease severity and histopathological damage only where baseline communities carried higher diversity and more complex co-occurrence architecture; in those animals the consortium preserved community structure and metabolic output, restoring disease-disrupted metabolites, and selectively raising butyrate and propionate. Sustained exogenous D-lactate did not abolish protection, placing D-lactate as a tractable readout of ecological restoration rather than its effector. Responsiveness is encoded in the baseline microbiota and predictable before intervention, establishing probiotic efficacy as a stratifiable property of the host microbiome.


Li J, Özkurt AG, Baertschi I, Wang J, Aeschlimann L, Goepfert C, Misselwitz B, Sokollik C, Yilmaz B


DOI: 10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118228  |  View on PubMed →





A microbiome-reactive TMIGD2hi Th17 subset is spatially enriched at the intestinal epithelium and expanded in inflammatory bowel disease.  Immunity  |  2026-10-26



Subsets of intestinal CD4+ T cells directly recognize commensal bacteria and coordinate tolerance versus protective immunity. Our limited understanding of CD4+ T cell specificities and corresponding functional phenotypes has created a barrier to deciphering the mechanisms of mucosal homeostasis and inflammation mediated by the adaptive immune system. To address this, we leveraged an immunodominant Bacteroidetes epitope in SusC to perform single-cell profiling of the SusC-specific and total CD4+ T cell landscapes in intestinal tissues of patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). By analyzing phenotypes and T cell receptor specificities in parallel, we uncovered phenotypic diversification of T helper 17 (Th17) cells in IBD and identified an epithelial-localized, SusC-reactive Th17 subset that is BACH2lo, GZMAhi, and expresses the costimulatory receptor TMIGD2. Together, our results highlight the utility of tracking commensal-specific T cell responses to define specialized subsets of Th17 cells associated with loss of tolerance to the microbiome.


Pedersen TK, Jain T, Segerstolpe Å, Lin C, Shih AR, Yuan L, Ashenberg O, Kaper ME, Twardus SW, Ricciardi R


DOI: 10.1016/j.immuni.2026.09.026  |  View on PubMed →





The intestinal microbiome in inflammatory bowel disease and spondyloarthritides.Review  Communications medicine  |  2026-10-24



Extraintestinal manifestations (EIMs) of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) can affect any organ system, ranging in presentation, frequency, and severity; the most common EIM is IBD-associated arthritis (IAA), an inflammatory arthritis affecting both axial and peripheral joints. IAA is a form of seronegative spondyloarthritis (SpA), which includes multiple arthritides, and those with IAA are also likelier to have other clinical features observed in those with SpA without IBD, such as increased rates of uveitis, psoriasis, and HLA-B27 positivity. These overlapping features are not limited to clinical disease features; the microbiome has been heavily implicated in the development of both IBD and SpA and is associated with non-SpA EIMs. In this review, we offer an overview of several bacterial taxa and associated metabolites that have been identified as differentially abundant in both IBD and SpA, both in stool and mucosal assessment, and how these taxa are associated with differences in intestinal permeability and immune profiles. We also describe how the overlapping dysbiotic microbiome and associated metabolome in IBD, EIMs of IBD, and SpA may differentially modulate the immune system, thus contributing to the shared underlying etiopathogenesis of these diseases. Further work is needed to characterize causal, mechanistic relationships beyond pure computationally identified associations, and apply these findings towards targeted therapeutic intervention and personalized medicine in IBD.


Alizadeh M, Siaton BC, Hudhud D, von Rosenvinge EC, Cross RK, Ravel J


DOI: 10.1038/s43856-026-01919-6  |  View on PubMed →





Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis C-2 Alleviates DSS-induced Ulcerative Colitis via the Microbiota-tryptophan Metabolism-AhR Pathway.  Probiotics and antimicrobial proteins  |  2026-10-24



Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic intestinal disorder closely linked to gut microbiota dysbiosis and metabolic disturbances. This study investigated the alleviating effects and mechanisms of Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis C-2 (C-2) on dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced ulcerative colitis (UC) in mice. Background: Increased intestinal permeability is a proposed pathophysiological mechanism in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), and zonulin, a putative regulator of tight junctions, has been investigated as a non-invasive serum biomarker. However, the diagnostic utility of circulating zonulin in IBS remains controversial. Objectives: To systematically review studies comparing serum or plasma zonulin concentrations between adult IBS patients and healthy controls, and to evaluate the influence of assay methodology on reported outcomes. Methods: A systematic literature search of PubMed was performed up to April 2026; the most recent eligible study was published in June 2024. Studies that enrolled adults with IBS diagnosed by Rome criteria, included healthy control groups, and measured zonulin by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) were eligible. Studies lacking a healthy control group, non-original reports, animal studies, and mixed functional gastrointestinal disorder cohorts without extractable IBS data were excluded. Findings were synthesised narratively due to substantial methodological heterogeneity and concerns regarding the validity of commercially available zonulin kits. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for case-control studies; six studies were at low risk and two at intermediate risk. The review is reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement, and this abstract follows the PRISMA 2020 for Abstracts checklist. Results: Eight case-control studies were included, comprising 421 IBS patients and 428 controls. Of the seven studies contributing to the primary synthesis, two reported significantly elevated zonulin in IBS, one produced opposite results with two different assays applied to the same samples, and four found no significant difference compared with controls. An eighth study, which combined IBS with inflammatory bowel disease and did not report IBS-specific data, was retained as supportive, non-primary evidence. Crucially, the studies employed different ELISA kits (ALPCO, Cusabio, Immundiagnostik, Zellbio) and different units of measurement. Independent validation studies have demonstrated that the most frequently used commercial kits do not recognise the pre-haptoglobin-2 molecule claimed to be zonulin, but instead detect haptoglobin, complement C3, or properdin. The only study employing a monoclonal antibody specific for pre-haptoglobin-2 observed lower, rather than higher, concentrations in IBS. Conclusions: The existing literature based on commercial ELISAs cannot determine whether pre-HP2/zonulin is altered in IBS, and the single genotype-controlled monoclonal assay suggests lower, not higher, concentrations in IBS. The disparate results are largely attributable to the application of ELISA kits that lack analytical specificity for the proposed target. Future research must use analytically validated assays, such as monoclonal antibody-based methods with concomitant genotyping for haptoglobin polymorphisms, before zonulin can be considered a meaningful biomarker in IBS.
